content: Cefprozil is a second-generation cephalosporin antibiotic that has been approved by the FDA for the treatment of mild to moderate infections. These include infections of the upper and lower respiratory tracts, as well as uncomplicated skin and skin-structure infections. Common side effects associated with cefprozil include diarrhea, nausea, elevated liver enzymes (ALT/SGPT and AST/SGOT), and vaginitis. Adult Indications and Dosage Cefprozil is prescribed for adults to treat infections caused by susceptible microorganisms. The specific conditions and dosages are as follows: 1. Pharyngitis/Tonsillitis caused by Streptococcus pyogenes: Dosage: 500 mg once daily for 10 days. 2. Otitis Media caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae (including β-lactamase-producing strains), and Moraxella catarrhalis (including β-lactamase-producing strains): Dosage: 500 mg every 12 hours for 10 days. 3. Acute Sinusitis caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae (including β-lactamase-producing strains), and Moraxella catarrhalis (including β-lactamase-producing strains): Dosage: 250 mg every 12 hours for 10 days. 4. Secondary Bacterial Infections of Acute Bronchitis and Acute Bacterial Exacerbation of Chronic Bronchitis caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae (including β-lactamase-producing strains), and Moraxella catarrhalis (including β-lactamase-producing strains): Dosage: 500 mg every 12 hours for 10 days. 5. Skin and Skin-Structure Infections caused by Staphylococcus aureus (including penicillinase-producing strains) and Streptococcus pyogenes: Dosage options: 250 mg every 12 hours for 10 days, or 500 mg once daily for 10 days, or 500 mg every 12 hours for 10 days. Note: Abscesses may require surgical drainage in addition to antibiotic therapy. Pediatric Indications and Dosage Cefprozil is also approved for use in children for the treatment of mild to moderate infections caused by susceptible microorganisms. The specific conditions and dosages are as follows: 1. Pharyngitis/Tonsillitis caused by Streptococcus pyogenes: Dosage for children aged 2–12 years: 7.5 mg/kg once daily for 10 days. 2. Otitis Media caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae (including β-lactamase-producing strains), and Moraxella catarrhalis (including β-lactamase-producing strains): Dosage for children aged 6 months–12 years: 15 mg/kg every 12 hours for 10 days. 3. Acute Sinusitis caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae (including β-lactamase-producing strains), and Moraxella catarrhalis (including β-lactamase-producing strains): Dosage for children aged 6 months–12 years: 7.5 mg/kg once daily for 10 days, or 15 mg/kg every 12 hours for 10 days. 4. Skin and Skin-Structure Infections caused by Staphylococcus aureus (including penicillinase-producing strains) and Streptococcus pyogenes: Dosage for children aged 2–12 years: 20 mg/kg once daily for 10 days. Note: Abscesses may require surgical drainage in addition to antibiotic therapy. Contraindications Cefprozil is contraindicated in patients with a known allergy to cephalosporin antibiotics. Warnings Before initiating therapy with cefprozil, it is essential to assess the patient’s history of hypersensitivity reactions to cefprozil, cephalosporins, penicillins, or other drugs. Cross-sensitivity among β-lactam antibiotics, including cephalosporins and penicillins, has been documented and may occur in up to 10% of patients with a history of penicillin allergy. If an allergic reaction occurs, cefprozil should be discontinued immediately. Severe hypersensitivity reactions may require emergency treatment, including epinephrine, oxygen, intravenous fluids, antihistamines, corticosteroids, pressor amines, and airway management. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including cefprozil. This condition can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use, even if it occurs up to two months after therapy. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, discontinuation of ongoing antibiotic therapy not directed against C. difficile may be necessary, along with appropriate management of fluids, electrolytes, and protein supplementation. Adverse Reactions The most common adverse effects observed in clinical trials include: Gastrointestinal: Diarrhea (2.9%), nausea (3.5%), vomiting (1%), and abdominal pain (1%). Hepatobiliary: Elevated liver enzymes, including AST (2%), ALT (2%), and alkaline phosphatase (0.2%). Rare cases of cholestatic jaundice have been reported. Hypersensitivity: Rash (0.9%) and urticaria (0.1%), more commonly observed in children. Central Nervous System: Dizziness (1%), hyperactivity, headache, nervousness, insomnia, confusion, and somnolence (all <1%). Hematologic: Eosinophilia (2.3%) and decreased leukocyte count (0.2%). Renal: Elevated BUN and serum creatinine (both 0.1%). Other: Diaper rash, superinfection (1.5%), genital pruritus, and vaginitis (1.6%). Rare but serious adverse events reported post-marketing include anaphylaxis, angioedema, colitis (including pseudomembranous colitis), Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and thrombocytopenia. Drug Interactions Concomitant use of cefprozil with aminoglycosides may increase the risk of nephrotoxicity. Co-administration with probenecid doubles the area under the curve (AUC) for cefprozil. The bioavailability of cefprozil is not affected by antacids when administered five minutes apart. Use in Specific Populations Pregnancy: Classified as Category B by the FDA. Animal studies have not shown harm to the fetus, but there are no adequate studies in pregnant women. Use only if clearly needed. Nursing Mothers: Small amounts of cefprozil (<0.3% of the dose) are excreted in breast milk. Caution is advised when administering to lactating women. Pediatric Use: Safety and efficacy have been established for children aged 6 months and older for otitis media and acute sinusitis, and for children aged 2 years and older for pharyngitis/tonsillitis and skin infections. Geriatric Use: No significant differences in safety or efficacy have been observed in elderly patients compared to younger adults. However, dose adjustments may be necessary in patients with impaired renal function. Renal Impairment: Dosage adjustments are required in patients with renal impairment to avoid prolonged plasma concentrations. Administration and Monitoring Cefprozil is administered orally. Monitoring renal function is recommended in patients with renal impairment or those receiving concurrent treatment with potent diuretics. Overdosage In cases of severe overdose, particularly in patients with renal impairment, hemodialysis may help remove cefprozil from the body. Pharmacokinetics Cefprozil is well-absorbed orally, with approximately 95% bioavailability. The plasma half-life is 1.3 hours in healthy individuals. The drug is primarily excreted by the kidneys, with approximately 60% of the dose recovered in the urine. Storage Cefprozil tablets should be stored at 20° to 25°C (68° to 77°F).
